title: 1. Introduction

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Watch a diffusion model generate an image and the picture comes into focus in a recognisable order. First there is a blur of colour, then a rough layout, then an object, and finally fine texture. Somewhere in the middle of this process the model commits . Before that moment, the half-finished image could still turn into several different things. After it, the outcome is settled: it will be a horse, and no amount of further sampling noise will turn it into a truck. Knowing when this happens is useful. It tells us where in the noise schedule guidance should act ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , where the class balance of generated data is decided, and which errors in a learned model actually change what gets drawn. It also connects to a line of theory. For simple data such as a mixture of two Gaussian blobs, the moment of commitment is a sharp event that physicists would call a phase transition ( Raya and Ambrogioni, 2023 ; Biroli and Mézard, 2023 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Li and Chen, 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2025 ) . Measuring commitment in a real, trained model raises two practical questions that the theory hides. Whose commitment do we mean? One option is to look at the whole population of half-finished images and ask when they visibly split into two groups, for example “cat-like” and “dog-like”. That is cheap, but what you see depends on how you choose to measure “cat-likeness”. The other option is to look at one image at a time and ask how certain its eventual outcome already is. That is exact, but expensive. We use both and check one against the other. Compared with what? A model can only commit “wrongly” relative to its training data. So we need a fair way to compare the model’s behaviour with the data’s, and evidence that this comparison would actually notice an error if one existed. We study CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) , with NVIDIA’s EDM models ( Karras et al., 2022 ) as the main subject and the original DDPM model ( Ho et al., 2020 ) as a second, older model family. Our findings are: 1. Coarse decisions come first. An image settles “vehicle or animal?” at about twice the noise level at which it settles “which animal?” (1.75–2.5 times, depending on how strictly “settled” is defined). The cheap population-level measurement puts class pairs in the right order (rank correlation 0.73–0.88), but its absolute timing depends on an arbitrary choice of scale, so we use it only for ordering (Section 5 ). 2. The comparison is fair, and it can see errors. On a toy problem where the right answer is known, it recovers that answer exactly. When we deliberately plant small errors in the data, it detects them (Sections 3.3 and 3.5 ). 3. EDM commits like its data, except for class proportions. Reweighting the data to match how often the model generates each class reproduces the model’s behaviour pair by pair, as closely as two halves of the data agree with each other. A class-conditional EDM model sampled with equal numbers of each class matches the data with no reweighting at all (Section 6 ). 4. Fixing the proportions fixes the commitment. Gently steering the sampler towards the right class proportions, with a classifier and no tuning, makes the model’s commitment match the data, and FID does not get worse (Section 7 ). 5. Part of “the model’s” imbalance belongs to the sampler. A 256-step stochastic sampler roughly doubles the class imbalance compared with the same network sampled more carefully (Section 6.4 ). 6. A weaker model makes an additional error. DDPM shows the same class-proportion effect, but it also commits about 20% too late, an error that is not about proportions at all (Section 8 ). sections.heading: 2. Two Ways to Describe Commitment
sections.text: Diffusion models in one paragraph. Take a clean image x 0 x_{0} and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ \sigma : x σ = x 0 + σ ​ ε x_{\sigma}=x_{0}+\sigma\varepsilon . A diffusion model is a network D ⁡ ( x , σ ) D(x,\sigma) trained to guess the clean image from the noisy one, that is, D ⁡ ( x , σ ) ≈ 𝔼 ⁡ [ x 0 ∣ x σ = x ] D(x,\sigma)\approx\mathbb{E}[x_{0}\mid x_{\sigma}=x] . From this guess one can compute the score , the direction in which noisy images become more likely: ∇ log ⁡ p σ ​ ( x ) = ( D ⁡ ( x , σ ) − x ) / σ 2 \nabla\log p_{\sigma}(x)=(D(x,\sigma)-x)/\sigma^{2} . To generate an image, start from pure noise at a large σ \sigma and repeatedly move along the score while lowering σ \sigma . This can be done deterministically, by following an ordinary differential equation (the probability-flow ODE), or with some fresh noise injected at every step (the reverse-time SDE) ( Song et al., 2021 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . With a perfect score, both produce samples from the training distribution. They differ in a way that will matter in Section 3.3 . The committor: one image at a time. Pause the stochastic sampler at some noise level σ \sigma and take the half-finished image x x . Now restart generation from x x many times, each time with different random noise, and look at what comes out. If 11 of 12 restarts end as a horse, the image is nearly committed to “horse”. If the outcomes are spread over several classes, it is not yet committed. The probability q c ​ ( x , σ ) q_{c}(x,\sigma) that a restart ends in class c c is the committor , a term from the study of rare transitions in chemistry and physics ( E and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010 ) . It describes a single image, needs no choice of measuring stick, and can be estimated simply by counting outcomes. Its drawback is cost, since every estimate needs many restarts. One fact makes it especially useful: for a perfect model, the committor of a noisy image is exactly the posterior probability of each class given that noisy image, P ⁡ ( c ∣ x σ = x ) P(c\mid x_{\sigma}=x) , under the training data (Appendix A.3 ). A classifier trained on noisy data estimates that posterior, so we can check whether a model’s committor matches what the data say it should be. The density transition: the whole population at once. The cheaper description looks at many images together. For a pair of classes, say cat ( a a ) and dog ( b b ), pick a single number m m that says how cat-like versus dog-like an image is, scaled so that clean cats sit near + 1 +1 and clean dogs near − 1 -1 . We call m m an order parameter . At high noise, every image looks equally ambiguous, and the distribution of m m over many noisy images has a single hump in the middle. At low noise, the cats and dogs separate, and the distribution has two humps. The noise level at which the second hump first appears is the density transition σ bif \sigma_{\rm bif} . Pitchforks and folds. How does one hump become two? Figure 1 shows the two possibilities. If the two classes are perfect mirror images (same size, same spread), the hump splits evenly into two, a pitchfork . If they are not, which is always the case for real data, the hump drifts towards one class and simply becomes it, and the other class appears later, suddenly, as a new hump. This is a fold . Folds are the generic case ( Stančević and Ambrogioni, 2026 ; Achilli et al., 2026 ; Marta and Causin, 2026 ) . Both shapes are captured by one simple formula. Write f ⁡ ( m ) f(m) for the slope of the log-distribution of m m ; it is positive to the left of a hump and negative to its right. Near the split, f ⁡ ( m ) ≈ h + a ​ m − b ​ m 3 , b > 0 , f(m)\approx h+a\,m-b\,m^{3},\qquad b>0, (1) which is the textbook “cusp” normal form ( Golubitsky and Schaeffer, 1985 ; Strogatz, 2018 ) . Each coefficient has a plain meaning. a a measures how strongly the noise is pushing the classes apart, and it grows as noise is removed. b b keeps the two humps at a finite distance. h h measures how lopsided the split is. With h = 0 h=0 the split is a pitchfork. With h ≠ 0 h\neq 0 it is a fold, and the second hump appears exactly when 4 ​ a 3 = 27 ​ b ​ h 2 . 4a^{3}=27\,b\,h^{2}. Suppose one class is generated more often than the other. In Figure 1 b, that is exactly what makes the split lopsided: the majority class wins the single hump. The effect can be made precise. If m m is a log-likelihood ratio, i.e. a well-calibrated classifier’s log-odds, then changing the class proportions from w a : w b w_{a}{:}w_{b} shifts h h by half the change in log ⁡ ( w a / w b ) \log(w_{a}/w_{b}) (Appendix A.5 ). So | h | = 0.08 |h|=0.08 is the lopsidedness that a 54/46 class split would produce. Equation ( 2 ) then adds a second consequence. A more lopsided split (larger | h | |h| ) needs a stronger push (larger a a ) before the second hump can appear, so it happens later in generation, at a lower noise level: Δ ​ log ⁡ σ bif ≈ − 3 ​ ( b / 4 ) 1 / 3 s ​ Δ ​ | h | 2 / 3 , s = − d ​ a d ​ log ⁡ σ . \Delta\log\sigma_{\rm bif}\;\approx\;-\frac{3\,(b/4)^{1/3}}{s}\;\Delta|h|^{2/3},\qquad s=-\frac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}\log\sigma}. (3) This is a useful sanity check, but it carries a warning. Any model that generates the wrong class proportions will show linked errors in lopsidedness and in timing, whatever else is wrong with it . Seeing those linked errors therefore cannot prove that proportions are the only problem. The decisive test, in Section 6 , is to give the data the model’s proportions and check whether everything else then matches.

sections.heading: 3.1. Committors, by restarting generation
sections.text: We generate 320 images with the unconditional EDM model, using the stochastic sampler. We pause each one at 12 noise levels between 7.9 7.9 and 0.1 0.1 , spaced by a factor of about 1.5 1.5 . From every paused image we restart generation 12 times, 46,080 restarts in all, and identify the class of each finished image with a separate, highly accurate classifier: a Vision Transformer fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) , with 98.4% test accuracy. We say a trajectory has decided its superclass (vehicle or animal) or its class at a noise level if at least 11 of the 12 restarts from that level, and from every lower level, agree with its own final outcome. For a pair of classes we pool information across trajectories. Among all trajectories that end as a a or b b , we look at the restarts that land in a a or b b and ask what fraction land on the other class of the pair. We call this the cross-over rate. A pair is decided below the noise level from which the cross-over rate stays under a threshold. We report three thresholds ( 0.05 0.05 , 0.1 0.1 and 0.2 0.2 ), because the exact noise level depends on how strict one is. We tested this procedure on a toy problem with six Gaussian classes, where committors are known exactly (Appendix C ). The pooled estimate matches its exact target with no bias from using only 12 restarts. Different reasonable definitions of “decided” differ by about one step of our noise grid.

sections.heading: 3.2. Density transitions, with a classifier as the measuring stick
sections.text: To measure how cat-like versus dog-like a noisy image is, we need an order parameter. For simple data like handwritten digits, a straight line through pixel space works. For CIFAR-10 it does not: along the best straight lines, the classes overlap so much that the distribution never shows two humps (Appendix E ). So we use a classifier. We train a ResNet that takes a noisy image and its noise level and outputs class probabilities (85% accurate on nearly clean test images, 64% at σ = 1 \sigma=1 ). For a pair of classes, the order parameter is the classifier’s log-odds z = ℓ a − ℓ b z=\ell_{a}-\ell_{b} , rescaled at each noise level so that the average a a sits at + 1 +1 and the average b b at − 1 -1 . We estimate the distribution of z z across noisy images with a smooth histogram (a kernel density estimate), scan 56 noise levels from high to low until a second hump appears, and fit Equation ( 1 ) there to read off h h . Two details keep the numbers honest. First, statistics that pool many pairs need special care: each class appears in nine of the 45 pairs, so the pairs are not independent. Our confidence intervals therefore resample whole classes ( class-block intervals , 1,000 resamples), and per-pair estimates are medians of 100 bootstrap resamples. Second, an estimated h h is never exactly zero, so we need to know how large it can be by chance. We built pairs of image sets that are exactly symmetric by construction: a class and its vertical flip, or a class and a copy with red and blue channels swapped. We passed them through a classifier trained on them. They give | h | |h| up to 0.047 0.047 , which serves as our noise floor (Appendix D ). The classifier is a measuring stick, and the scale of the stick matters. If we replaced the log-odds z z by a squashed version such as tanh ⁡ ( z / 2 ) \tanh(z/2) , every density transition would move, by a median factor of 4.5 4.5 . What does not depend on the stick is the ordering of class pairs, which is stable across two very different classifier architectures ( r = 0.96 r=0.96 ) and a recalibration ( r = 0.97 r=0.97 ). Nor does any comparison between a model and its data made with the same stick , because two identical distributions look identical under any stick. We rely only on these robust quantities.

sections.heading: 3.3. Comparing a model with its data
sections.text: To compare a model with its training data, we record the classifier’s log-odds along the model’s generation trajectories and compare them with the log-odds of real images that have had noise added to them. This is only fair if a perfect model would give exactly the same result as the data. For the stochastic sampler it does: Proposition 1 . Let w c w_{c} be any classifier’s probability for class c c on nearly clean images (noise level σ min \sigma_{\min} ), and let σ > σ min \sigma>\sigma_{\min} . With a perfect score, the distribution of ϕ ⁡ ( x σ ) \phi(x_{\sigma}) along reverse-SDE trajectories, with each trajectory weighted by w a + w b w_{a}+w_{b} at its end point, equals the distribution of ϕ ⁡ ( x σ ) \phi(x_{\sigma}) obtained by adding noise to real images, with each image weighted by w a + w b w_{a}+w_{b} at σ min \sigma_{\min} . The intuition is that the stochastic sampler, run with a perfect score, is the noising process played backwards in time ( Anderson, 1982 ; Haussmann and Pardoux, 1986 ) . Any statement about how an image at one noise level relates to the same image at another noise level is therefore identical on both sides (Appendix A.3 ). The deterministic ODE sampler does not have this property: it produces the right distribution at each noise level, but it links noise levels together differently. We confirmed both facts on a toy problem with three Gaussian classes and an exactly known score. The SDE comparison returns a ratio of 1.00 1.00 ( [ 0.94 , 1.07 ] [0.94,1.07] ), meaning no difference, while the ODE returns 1.36 1.36 ( [ 1.20 , 1.54 ] [1.20,1.54] ). Model and data are always compared at the same sample size, because the smoothing in our histograms depends on it. Two kinds of reweighting appear below. Rebalancing rescales the model’s samples so that the two classes of a pair carry equal weight. Mass-matching goes the other way: it reweights the data so that its class proportions equal the model’s. The second is the cleaner test, because it leaves the model untouched.

sections.heading: 3.4. A check of the measuring pipeline
sections.text: If the pipeline works, changing class proportions by a known amount should change h h by half the change in log class ratio, regardless of any model. We checked this on the data alone, reweighting the test images by random known class factors. The slope was 1.00 1.00 ( r = 0.98 r=0.98 , over the 38 pairs whose split was detected both before and after reweighting). Imposing a known imbalance on the model through guidance gave a slope of 1.05 1.05 . These numbers confirm that the classifier behaves like a calibrated likelihood ratio and that the cubic fit is accurate. They say nothing about whether any model is right.

sections.heading: 3.5. Can the comparison see errors?
sections.text: Figure 2: Can the comparison detect errors? We distort the real data on purpose, by reweighting images within each class towards more typical-looking examples. Class proportions stay unchanged. We then compare distorted with clean data exactly as we compare a model with data. The horizontal axis is the size of the distortion (KL divergence, nats per class). (a) Ratio of split noise levels, averaged over pairs, with class-block intervals: the timing of the split reacts to small distortions. (b) Agreement of the lopsidedness h h : it barely reacts until the distortion is large. Blue: all classes distorted; red: only deer. A test that always says “looks fine” is worthless. To find out what ours can and cannot see, we planted errors on purpose. Within each class, we reweighted real images towards the more typical-looking ones, which makes classes tighter, without changing how many images each class has. Then we compared the distorted data with clean data, exactly as we compare a model with data (Figure 2 ). The two quantities we measure turn out to be very different in sensitivity. • The timing of the split is sensitive. A distortion of only 0.027 0.027 nats per class moves split noise levels by a factor of 1.18 1.18 ( [ 1.10 , 1.26 ] [1.10,1.26] ). • The lopsidedness is not. Its agreement with clean data stays at 0.98 0.98 for distortions up to 0.12 0.12 nats, and drops to 0.88 0.88 only at 0.53 0.53 nats. • A distortion in one class shows up mainly in that class’s pairs. Distorting deer alone barely moves the average timing, but it increases the spread across pairs and changes the lopsidedness of several deer pairs. One limitation is built in. The classifier only looks along the “which class is it?” direction, so errors in other aspects of images, such as texture or style within a class, are invisible to this test.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Setup
sections.text: This section collects every detail needed to reproduce our experiments; the code is available at https://github.com/nssprogrammer/diffusion-commit . Further details, and the checks behind several choices, are in the appendices. Data. All experiments use CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) : 50,000 training and 10,000 test images of 32 × 32 32\times 32 pixels in ten classes, with pixel values scaled to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . Noise levels σ \sigma are on this scale. The data reference for every comparison is the test set, with four independent noise draws per image (40,000 noisy images per noise level), so the classifier is never evaluated on images it was trained on. Classifiers. We use four classifiers, each for a different job. • The census classifier defines the order parameter. It is a ResNet with an input convolution of 64 channels and five residual blocks (64, 128, 128, 256 and 256 channels, two with stride 2), with BatchNorm and SiLU activations. It takes the noise level through a sinusoidal embedding of 1 4 ​ log ⁡ σ \frac{1}{4}\log\sigma , followed by a small MLP and a scale-and-shift (FiLM) in every block ( Perez et al., 2018 ) . It is trained on the training set for 25 epochs with AdamW (learning rate 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} on a one-cycle schedule, weight decay 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , batch size 256), with horizontal flips and noise levels drawn log-uniformly between 0.05 0.05 and 10 10 . Its test accuracy is 85.2%, 81.8%, 76.0%, 64.2%, 48.6% and 34.4% at σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 , 0.25 0.25 , 0.5 0.5 , 1 1 , 2 2 and 4 4 . • A second architecture checks that results do not depend on the census classifier. It is a plain VGG-style network with GroupNorm, which takes the noise level by rescaling its input by 1 / 1 + σ 2 1/\sqrt{1+\sigma^{2}} and appending 1 4 ​ log ⁡ σ \frac{1}{4}\log\sigma as an extra input channel. • The null classifier has the census architecture with 30 outputs: the ten classes, their vertical flips, and their red–blue channel swaps. It is used only to build the noise floor of Section 3.2 . • The labelling classifier labels finished images: a ViT-Base fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 at 224 × 224 224\times 224 resolution ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) , with 98.4% test accuracy. It is independent of everything else in the pipeline. Diffusion models. NVIDIA’s pretrained EDM checkpoints for CIFAR-10 ( Karras et al., 2022 , unconditional and class-conditional, VP preconditioning, 56M parameters;) , and the original DDPM checkpoint ( Ho et al., 2020 ) . DDPM is wrapped as described in Section 8 . Samplers. Unless stated otherwise, we sample with the reverse-time SDE using 256 Euler–Maruyama steps on the EDM noise schedule (exponent ρ = 7 \rho=7 ), from σ = 80 \sigma=80 down to σ min = 0.05 \sigma_{\min}=0.05 , in half precision, and finish with one denoising step. For comparison we also use EDM’s standard deterministic Heun sampler (18 steps, 35 network evaluations, down to σ = 0.002 \sigma=0.002 ) and the stochastic sampler with 512 and 1,024 steps, all in full precision. Recording. Along every generated trajectory we record the census classifier’s logits at the 68 schedule steps between σ = 7.95 \sigma=7.95 and σ = 0.086 \sigma=0.086 . At the end, the classifier’s class probabilities at σ min \sigma_{\min} give each trajectory a weight for each class. Data-reference images are treated identically: noised first to σ min \sigma_{\min} (for their class weights) and then onwards (for their logits). Density transitions. For each class pair, the log-odds are standardised at each noise level using the data reference, so that the two class means sit at ± 1 \pm 1 , and the same standardisation is applied to the model. The distribution is estimated with a Gaussian kernel density (bandwidth 1.5 times Silverman’s rule) on a grid of 4,001 points over [ − 4 , 4 ] [-4,4] . Peaks closer than 0.03 0.03 , or separated by less than 0.05 0.05 nats of log-density, are merged. The census scans 56 noise levels, spaced logarithmically from 20 down to 0.08 0.08 . Model comparisons scan the 68 recorded levels. The transition σ bif \sigma_{\rm bif} is the first level with two peaks after at least one level with a single peak. The asymmetry h h comes from a density-weighted fit of Equation ( 1 ) over | m | < 1 |m|<1 at that level. Committors. We use 320 trajectories of the unconditional EDM model, paused at 12 noise levels between 7.95 7.95 and 0.099 0.099 , with 12 restarts from each paused image (46,080 restarts). Finished images are labelled by the ViT. Decisions use the 11-of-12 rule for superclass and class, and pooled cross-over rates with thresholds 0.05 0.05 , 0.1 0.1 and 0.2 0.2 for pairs. A level counts only if at least 20 restarts landed in the pair. Table 2: All sampling runs. “Images” is the number of generated trajectories. The class-proportion correction of Equation ( 4 ) uses the census classifier at every sampling step. Its target is the classifier’s class proportions on the test set, and the model’s proportions come from the main run. The second round raises the target for each class by the ratio by which the first round fell short. Per-pair values are medians of bootstrap resamples within each class: 100 for the main comparisons, 60 for planted errors and 30 for corruptions. Census intervals per pair use 1,000 resamples. Multiple testing over pairs is controlled with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at 5%. Reliability ceilings use split halves and the Spearman–Brown formula. Model and data are always compared at the same sample size. Image quality. FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) uses Inception pool features of the generated images against the 50,000 training images. Because FID is biased upwards at small sample sizes, we compare FID only between runs of the same size. Hardware and software. All experiments ran on a single NVIDIA T4 GPU (16 GB) in cloud notebooks, about 80 GPU-hours in total, using PyTorch. The statistical re-analyses ran on CPU. Appendix L breaks down compute and lists dataset and checkpoint licences.

Individual images settle “vehicle or animal?” below a median noise level of 2.4 2.4 , and their exact class below 1.1 1.1 (Figure 3 a). Pair by pair, vehicle/animal pairs such as airplane/frog are decided at 1.8–2.5 times the noise level of animal/animal pairs such as cat/deer, depending on the threshold (Table 3 ). This coarse-to-fine order agrees with earlier observations on trained models ( Handke et al., 2025 ; Sclocchi et al., 2025 ) and with theory for data with nested classes ( Achilli et al., 2026 ) . A pair can sometimes be decided before the coarser question. An image may have ruled out “automobile” while “truck” and “deer” are both still open. The cheap measurement gets the order right but not the timing. Density transitions and decision levels rank the 45 pairs in nearly the same order, with rank correlations of 0.73–0.88 for every threshold and both measuring sticks. Their ratio, however, depends on the stick. With the log-odds, density transitions come 1.6–4.2 times later than decisions, and more so for fine distinctions. With the squashed stick tanh ⁡ ( z / 2 ) \tanh(z/2) , which is the pairwise committor scale, the ratio is the same for all kinds of pairs and close to one at the loosest threshold. So the log-odds census in Figure 4 a, where vehicle/animal splits happen 5.8 5.8 times earlier than animal/animal splits (class-block interval [ 3.9 , 8.1 ] [3.9,8.1] ), exaggerates how strongly hierarchical commitment is. The order is real. Most of it can be predicted from simple image statistics: a Gaussian model built from each class’s average image and pixel covariance predicts the transitions with r = 0.89 r=0.89 . Splits are only mildly lopsided. The typical | h | |h| is 0.08 0.08 , the lopsidedness of a 54/46 class split. After correcting for testing 44 pairs at once (Benjamini–Hochberg at 5%), 19 pairs are more lopsided than the noise floor, and 12 remain so, with the same sign, under two different measuring sticks (Figure 4 b). sections.heading: 6. What the EDM Model Gets Wrong
sections.text: We now turn to NVIDIA’s pretrained unconditional EDM model for CIFAR-10 ( Karras et al., 2022 , 56M parameters;) . We sample it with the stochastic sampler (256 Euler–Maruyama steps, half precision), and also study its class-conditional sibling. The main run has 14,500 generated images, the others 2,500–4,000. Each is compared with the data at the same sample size. Figure 5: The unconditional EDM model, before any correction. (a) Density transition noise levels of the model against the data’s, with 95% bootstrap intervals; the dashed line is equality. (b) The model’s lopsidedness h h for each pair against the difference in how much the model over-produces the two classes. (c) How often each class is generated, relative to the test set, under our 256-step sampler and EDM’s standard 18-step sampler, as judged by our classifier and by an independent ViT.

sections.heading: 6.1. At first sight, the model looks only partly right
sections.text: The model generates some classes too often (horse, automobile) and others too rarely (bird, deer), as both classifiers agree (Figure 5 c). Its split noise levels scatter around the data’s, with no overall shift but a large spread across pairs: the standard deviation of the log ratio is 0.33 0.33 , against 0.21 0.21 between two halves of the data. Its lopsidedness is essentially unrelated to the data’s ( r = 0.11 r=0.11 ). Instead it follows the model’s own class imbalance: the class it over-produces is the class that wins the split ( r = 0.76 r=0.76 , Figure 5 b). The timing and lopsidedness errors are also linked as Equation ( 3 ) predicts (Figure 6 a). Their correlation is − 0.80 -0.80 (class-block interval [ − 0.92 , − 0.48 ] [-0.92,-0.48] ), and − 0.68 -0.68 when the two are measured on separate halves of the generated images, which rules out shared noise. The equation’s prediction, which has no free parameters, tracks the measured timing errors with r = 0.71 r=0.71 , though with a slope of 0.65 0.65 that we cannot fully explain. As Section 2 warned, all of this is what wrong class proportions would produce, whatever else is wrong. So it does not settle the question.

sections.heading: 6.3. A model that gets the proportions right by design
sections.text: The class-conditional EDM model can be told which class to draw. If we ask for equal numbers of each class, the class proportions are right by construction: their error by the ViT is 0.016 0.016 , below the 0.04 0.04 expected from sampling noise at this sample size. With no reweighting of any kind, this model splits at the same noise levels as the data (median ratio 1.00 1.00 , [ 0.92 , 1.18 ] [0.92,1.18] ), with a pair-to-pair spread of 0.223 0.223 against 0.211 0.211 between two halves of the data. Its lopsidedness agrees with the data’s at 0.87 0.87 .

sections.heading: 6.4. Is it the network or the sampler?
sections.text: Table 5: Class imbalance (average | log | |\log| of generated over expected frequency, by the ViT) of the same EDM network under different samplers. “Noise floor” is the value expected from random sampling alone at that sample size, with perfectly balanced classes. sampler precision images class imbalance noise floor stochastic, 256 steps half 2,500–3,500 0.12–0.15 0.040–0.048 stochastic, 256 steps full 2,000 0.171 0.054 stochastic, 512 steps full 1,500 0.132 0.063 stochastic, 1,024 steps full 1,000 0.137 0.076 deterministic, 18 steps (EDM default) full 10,000 0.095 0.024 How much of the imbalance belongs to the trained network and how much to our sampler? Some to each (Table 5 ). Numerical precision makes no difference. Taking more steps does: going from 256 to 512 steps reduces the imbalance, and going on to 1,024 steps does not reduce it further, which leaves it close to EDM’s standard deterministic sampler once sampling noise is accounted for. The same classes are over- and under-produced throughout. So the network itself has a class imbalance of roughly 10–15%, and our coarse 256-step sampler roughly doubles it. Since our comparisons concern the images actually generated, they hold either way. “The model” in this paper means the network together with its sampler. Similar skews have been reported for attributes such as gender and race in unconditional diffusion models trained on balanced face data ( Perera and Patel, 2023 ; Pal et al., 2023 ) . Here we see the same effect for classes, and we see exactly where it shows up during generation.

sections.heading: 7. Correcting the Class Proportions
sections.text: If the problem is class proportions, can we fix it during sampling? We can nudge the sampler towards target proportions f t f^{t} by adding a small correction to the score at every step. The exact correction depends on the model’s own class probabilities. Assuming, as the previous section supports, that the model’s classes have the right shapes and only the wrong proportions, those probabilities can be computed from a classifier trained on the data: ∇ x [ LSE c ⁡ ( ℓ c + log ⁡ f c t f c d ) − LSE c ⁡ ( ℓ c + log ⁡ f c m f c d ) ] . \nabla_{x}\Big[\operatorname{LSE}_{c}\big(\ell_{c}+\log\tfrac{f^{t}_{c}}{f^{d}_{c}}\big)-\operatorname{LSE}_{c}\big(\ell_{c}+\log\tfrac{f^{m}_{c}}{f^{d}_{c}}\big)\Big]. (4) Here ℓ c \ell_{c} are the classifier’s logits, f d f^{d} are the class proportions it was trained on, f m f^{m} those the model generates, and LSE is log-sum-exp. This is classifier guidance with a strength fixed by theory, so there is nothing to tune. An earlier version of this correction used the data’s class probabilities directly, which is right only to first order. sections.heading: 8. A Second Model: DDPM
sections.text: Is this story special to EDM? We ran the original DDPM model for CIFAR-10 ( Ho et al., 2020 ) through exactly the same pipeline. DDPM was trained with a different noise parameterisation, so we translate: at each noise level we use DDPM’s nearest training noise level and convert its noise prediction into a clean-image guess, D ⁡ ( x , σ ) = x − σ t ​ ε θ ​ ( x ​ α ¯ t , t ) D(x,\sigma)=x-\sigma_{t}\,\varepsilon_{\theta}(x\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}},t) with σ t = ( 1 − α ¯ t ) / α ¯ t \sigma_{t}=\sqrt{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})/\bar{\alpha}_{t}} . The noise levels differ by a median of 0.2 % 0.2\% , at most 1.3 % 1.3\% above σ = 0.1 \sigma=0.1 and 2.6 % 2.6\% at the very lowest levels. That is far below the 10 % 10\% mismatch that visibly changes commitment in our corruption experiments (Appendix H ). DDPM is much more imbalanced than EDM, with an imbalance of 0.29 0.29 by the ViT: frogs make up 19% of its images, dogs and ships about 6% each. The lopsidedness of DDPM’s splits is, again, entirely explained by its class proportions: against mass-matched data the agreement is 0.985 0.985 ( [ 0.89 , 1.00 ] [0.89,1.00] ), as good as between two halves of the data (Table 4 ). The timing is not. Even against mass-matched data, DDPM splits at 0.80 0.80 times the data’s noise level ( [ 0.66 , 0.93 ] [0.66,0.93] ), that is, later in generation, and with more pair-to-pair spread ( 0.31 0.31 against 0.21 0.21 ). Our planted-error test showed that timing reacts to distortions of a few hundredths of a nat per class. This looks like that kind of error, in the direction of classes that are broader and overlap more than they should. So the method does not simply pass every model. It tells apart a model whose only commitment error is class proportions from one that also commits late. Handke et al. (2025) measured the timing of class decisions in DDPM models on CIFAR-10 with an entropy-based method; our comparison adds a reference point from the data.

sections.heading: 9. Related Work
sections.text: Commitment in diffusion models. Speciation and critical windows have been analysed for mixtures and for data with nested classes ( Biroli and Mézard, 2023 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Raya and Ambrogioni, 2023 ; Li and Chen, 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2025 ; Achilli et al., 2026 ; Marta and Causin, 2026 ) . Stančević and Ambrogioni (2026) study the lopsided two-class case and entropy-based detectors. Handke et al. (2025) ; Handke et al. (2026) track class probabilities along the trajectories of trained models. Sclocchi et al. (2025) use forward–backward experiments, which are close in spirit to our restarts. Our contributions are measurements: committors placed side by side with density transitions, a model-versus-data comparison that is exact in principle and whose power we measure, and a breakdown of a trained model’s commitment errors into class proportions and, for a weaker model, timing. Measuring sticks and committors. That a landscape depends on the coordinate in which it is drawn is well known in molecular simulation ( Hartmann and Schütte, 2007 ) , where the committor is the standard coordinate-free alternative ( E and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010 ) . Following the peaks of a distribution as it is smoothed goes back to Silverman (1981) and Minnotte and Scott (1993) . Class balance in generative models. Counting the classes of generated images with a separate classifier goes back at least to Santurkar et al. (2018) . Unconditional diffusion models trained on balanced data have been found to skew attributes such as gender and race ( Perera and Patel, 2023 ; Pal et al., 2023 ) . Rebalancing through guidance is established ( Qin et al., 2023 ; Parihar et al., 2024 ) . Nicoletti et al. (2026) analyse how class spread and imbalance shape what a network learns first. The classes our EDM run over-produces tend to be those with more pixel variance (correlation 0.5 0.5 over ten classes), consistent with their analysis though not a test of it. Exposure bias ( Ning et al., 2024 ) concerns mismatches between the noisy images a sampler visits and those seen in training.

sections.heading: 10. Limitations
sections.text: • Scope. One dataset with ten classes, and two model families. Whether the same picture holds for larger datasets with deeper class hierarchies, such as ImageNet, is open. • What the method can see. Only commitment along the “which class?” direction, measured through a learned classifier. The lopsidedness measure is insensitive to distortions below about 0.5 0.5 nats per class, whereas the timing measure is much more sensitive. Errors unrelated to class identity are invisible. • Committors. 320 trajectories, 12 restarts each, and noise levels spaced by a factor of 1.5 1.5 . Decision levels move by about one grid step with the definition of “decided”. The small excess in committor fidelity is unexplained. • Left-overs. EDM’s 11% timing shift against mass-matched data has no mechanism we can identify, and after correction our intervals cannot tell whether it persists. Equation ( 3 ) predicts timing errors about a third larger than measured, also unexplained. • DDPM is run through our translation layer rather than its native sampler. • Correction. We could not determine on CIFAR-10 at which noise levels the correction must act. The claim that class ordering is mostly simple image statistics rests on a Gaussian prediction, not on generating from a Gaussian model.

sections.heading: 11. Conclusion
sections.text: So when does a diffusion model decide what to draw? On CIFAR-10, coarse decisions come first. An image settles whether it is a vehicle or an animal at about twice the noise level at which it settles which animal. And what does a strong model get wrong about these decisions? Remarkably little, along the class axis: it decides exactly as its data do, except that it draws some classes too often. Give the data the model’s class proportions and the data reproduce the model. Give the model the data’s proportions, through conditioning or a small, tuning-free correction to its sampler, and the model reproduces the data. A weaker model shows the same effect plus a delay in when it commits, which the same method picks up. The cheap way of measuring commitment puts decisions in the right order, but only the expensive way, restarting generation and counting outcomes, tells their time.

sections.heading: A.2. Why modes are not fixed points for nonlinear coordinates
sections.text: Under the reverse dynamics, a nonlinear ϕ \phi evolves with a drift and a diffusion coefficient. The Markovian projection onto m m has an effective diffusion D ⁡ ( m ) ∝ 𝔼 ⁡ [ | ∇ ϕ | 2 ∣ ϕ = m ] D(m)\propto\mathbb{E}[|\nabla\phi|^{2}\mid\phi=m] ( Gyöngy, 1986 ) . For a one-dimensional diffusion with drift μ ⁡ ( m ) \mu(m) and diffusion D ⁡ ( m ) D(m) , the stationary density satisfies μ = D ​ ( log ⁡ p ) ′ + D ′ \mu=D\,(\log p)^{\prime}+D^{\prime} . Zeros of the drift therefore coincide with modes of p p only when D D is constant, which holds for linear coordinates. For classifier coordinates, | ∇ ϕ | |\nabla\phi| varies strongly with m m , so we interpret the natural-image results as statements about the modes of a density, not about attractors.

sections.heading: Appendix G Committors: Protocol and Checks
sections.text: Protocol. We generated 320 trajectories with the same reverse SDE as in the main experiments and stored their states at the 12 schedule steps closest to a logarithmic grid between σ = 7.9 \sigma=7.9 and 0.10 0.10 (the levels of Table 11 ). From each stored state we ran 12 continuations with independent noise to σ min = 0.05 \sigma_{\min}=0.05 , denoised the end point, and labelled it with the ViT. The trajectories’ own final labels give the class frequencies; deer is the rarest at 4.4 % 4.4\% . At each stored state we also recorded our noise-conditional classifier’s posterior. A biased estimator, and its fix. Our first estimator of pairwise decisions considered a state only if at least six of its twelve continuations landed in the pair. At high noise that rule keeps only states that are already heading towards the pair, so it overstates commitment there. It gave median pair decisions of 3.7 3.7 – 5.4 5.4 , including animal pairs supposedly decided above the noise level at which animal-versus-vehicle is settled ( 2.4 2.4 ), which is impossible. sections.text: A common way to locate the critical window is the noise level at which the variance across samples of a conditional entropy peaks ( Stančević and Ambrogioni, 2026 ) . Its variance curve rises again above τ ≈ 3 \tau\approx 3 , where the posterior carries no information, and the maximum jumps to the edge of the grid; restricting the search to τ < 3 \tau<3 removes the outlier. Detectors of this kind therefore sit close to the population transition, and, by Section 3.1 , somewhat after individual samples have decided.

Snigdha Chandan Khilar Independent Researcher · snkhilar@gmail.com A diffusion model starts from pure noise and removes it step by step. Somewhere along the way it stops being able to become “anything” and becomes committed to, say, a horse rather than a truck. We measure when this happens, and what a trained model gets wrong about it, on CIFAR-10. The most direct measurement is to freeze a half-finished image, restart the generation from that point many times, and count how often each class comes out. We call this probability the committor. Measured this way, the model settles coarse questions (vehicle or animal?) at roughly twice the noise level of fine ones (which animal?). A much cheaper measurement, the noise level at which a classifier’s opinion about two classes splits into two distinct groups, gets the order of these decisions right (rank correlation 0.73–0.88) but not their exact timing. We then compare pretrained models with their training data, using a comparison that is exact in principle. For NVIDIA’s EDM model the result is simple: along the class axis, the model commits exactly as its data do, except that it generates some classes too often and others too rarely. If we give the data the model’s class proportions, the data reproduce the model’s behaviour pair by pair, as closely as two halves of the data reproduce each other. If we give the model the data’s proportions, by sampling a class-conditional model with uniform labels or by gently steering the sampler, the model reproduces the data’s behaviour, with no loss in image quality. Part of the class imbalance comes from the sampler rather than the network: a coarse 256-step sampler roughly doubles it. An older DDPM model shows the same class-proportion effect plus a second error, committing about 20% too late, which our planted-error tests show the method is able to detect. Code: https://github.com/nssprogrammer/diffusion-commit 1. Introduction Watch a diffusion model generate an image and the picture comes into focus in a recognisable order. First there is a blur of colour, then a rough layout, then an object, and finally fine texture. Somewhere in the middle of this process the model commits . Before that moment, the half-finished image could still turn into several different things. After it, the outcome is settled: it will be a horse, and no amount of further sampling noise will turn it into a truck. Knowing when this happens is useful. It tells us where in the noise schedule guidance should act ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , where the class balance of generated data is decided, and which errors in a learned model actually change what gets drawn. It also connects to a line of theory. For simple data such as a mixture of two Gaussian blobs, the moment of commitment is a sharp event that physicists would call a phase transition ( Raya and Ambrogioni, 2023 ; Biroli and Mézard, 2023 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Li and Chen, 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2025 ) . Measuring commitment in a real, trained model raises two practical questions that the theory hides. Whose commitment do we mean? One option is to look at the whole population of half-finished images and ask when they visibly split into two groups, for example “cat-like” and “dog-like”. That is cheap, but what you see depends on how you choose to measure “cat-likeness”. The other option is to look at one image at a time and ask how certain its eventual outcome already is. That is exact, but expensive. We use both and check one against the other. Compared with what? A model can only commit “wrongly” relative to its training data. So we need a fair way to compare the model’s behaviour with the data’s, and evidence that this comparison would actually notice an error if one existed. We study CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) , with NVIDIA’s EDM models ( Karras et al., 2022 ) as the main subject and the original DDPM model ( Ho et al., 2020 ) as a second, older model family. Our findings are: 1. Coarse decisions come first. An image settles “vehicle or animal?” at about twice the noise level at which it settles “which animal?” (1.75–2.5 times, depending on how strictly “settled” is defined). The cheap population-level measurement puts class pairs in the right order (rank correlation 0.73–0.88), but its absolute timing depends on an arbitrary choice of scale, so we use it only for ordering (Section 5 ). 2. The comparison is fair, and it can see errors. On a toy problem where the right answer is known, it recovers that answer exactly. When we deliberately plant small errors in the data, it detects them (Sections 3.3 and 3.5 ). 3. EDM commits like its data, except for class proportions. Reweighting the data to match how often the model generates each class reproduces the model’s behaviour pair by pair, as closely as two halves of the data agree with each other. A class-conditional EDM model sampled with equal numbers of each class matches the data with no reweighting at all (Section 6 ). 4. Fixing the proportions fixes the commitment. Gently steering the sampler towards the right class proportions, with a classifier and no tuning, makes the model’s commitment match the data, and FID does not get worse (Section 7 ). 5. Part of “the model’s” imbalance belongs to the sampler. A 256-step stochastic sampler roughly doubles the class imbalance compared with the same network sampled more carefully (Section 6.4 ). 6. A weaker model makes an additional error. DDPM shows the same class-proportion effect, but it also commits about 20% too late, an error that is not about proportions at all (Section 8 ). Take a clean image x 0 x_{0} and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ \sigma : x σ = x 0 + σ ​ ε x_{\sigma}=x_{0}+\sigma\varepsilon . A diffusion model is a network D ⁡ ( x , σ ) D(x,\sigma) trained to guess the clean image from the noisy one, that is, D ⁡ ( x , σ ) ≈ 𝔼 ⁡ [ x 0 ∣ x σ = x ] D(x,\sigma)\approx\mathbb{E}[x_{0}\mid x_{\sigma}=x] . To generate an image, start from pure noise at a large σ \sigma and repeatedly move along the score while lowering σ \sigma . This can be done deterministically, by following an ordinary differential equation (the probability-flow ODE), or with some fresh noise injected at every step (the reverse-time SDE) ( Song et al., 2021 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . With a perfect score, both produce samples from the training distribution. They differ in a way that will matter in Section 3.3 . The committor: one image at a time. Pause the stochastic sampler at some noise level σ \sigma and take the half-finished image x x . Now restart generation from x x many times, each time with different random noise, and look at what comes out. If 11 of 12 restarts end as a horse, the image is nearly committed to “horse”. If the outcomes are spread over several classes, it is not yet committed. The probability q c ​ ( x , σ ) q_{c}(x,\sigma) that a restart ends in class c c is the committor , a term from the study of rare transitions in chemistry and physics ( E and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010 ) . It describes a single image, needs no choice of measuring stick, and can be estimated simply by counting outcomes. Its drawback is cost, since every estimate needs many restarts. One fact makes it especially useful: for a perfect model, the committor of a noisy image is exactly the posterior probability of each class given that noisy image, P ⁡ ( c ∣ x σ = x ) P(c\mid x_{\sigma}=x) , under the training data (Appendix A.3 ). A classifier trained on noisy data estimates that posterior, so we can check whether a model’s committor matches what the data say it should be. The density transition: the whole population at once. The cheaper description looks at many images together. For a pair of classes, say cat ( a a ) and dog ( b b ), pick a single number m m that says how cat-like versus dog-like an image is, scaled so that clean cats sit near + 1 +1 and clean dogs near − 1 -1 . If the two classes are perfect mirror images (same size, same spread), the hump splits evenly into two, a pitchfork . Suppose one class is generated more often than the other. In Figure 1 b, that is exactly what makes the split lopsided: the majority class wins the single hump. The effect can be made precise. If m m is a log-likelihood ratio, i.e. a well-calibrated classifier’s log-odds, then changing the class proportions from w a : w b w_{a}{:}w_{b} shifts h h by half the change in log ⁡ ( w a / w b ) \log(w_{a}/w_{b}) (Appendix A.5 ). (3) This is a useful sanity check, but it carries a warning. Any model that generates the wrong class proportions will show linked errors in lopsidedness and in timing, whatever else is wrong with it . Seeing those linked errors therefore cannot prove that proportions are the only problem. The decisive test, in Section 6 , is to give the data the model’s proportions and check whether everything else then matches. 3. How We Measure 3.1. Committors, by restarting generation We generate 320 images with the unconditional EDM model, using the stochastic sampler. We pause each one at 12 noise levels between 7.9 7.9 and 0.1 0.1 , spaced by a factor of about 1.5 1.5 . From every paused image we restart generation 12 times, 46,080 restarts in all, and identify the class of each finished image with a separate, highly accurate classifier: a Vision Transformer fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) , with 98.4% test accuracy. We say a trajectory has decided its superclass (vehicle or animal) or its class at a noise level if at least 11 of the 12 restarts from that level, and from every lower level, agree with its own final outcome. For a pair of classes we pool information across trajectories. Among all trajectories that end as a a or b b , we look at the restarts that land in a a or b b and ask what fraction land on the other class of the pair. We call this the cross-over rate. A pair is decided below the noise level from which the cross-over rate stays under a threshold. We report three thresholds ( 0.05 0.05 , 0.1 0.1 and 0.2 0.2 ), because the exact noise level depends on how strict one is. We tested this procedure on a toy problem with six Gaussian classes, where committors are known exactly (Appendix C ). The pooled estimate matches its exact target with no bias from using only 12 restarts. Different reasonable definitions of “decided” differ by about one step of our noise grid. 3.2. Density transitions, with a classifier as the measuring stick To measure how cat-like versus dog-like a noisy image is, we need an order parameter. For simple data like handwritten digits, a straight line through pixel space works. For CIFAR-10 it does not: along the best straight lines, the classes overlap so much that the distribution never shows two humps (Appendix E ). So we use a classifier. We train a ResNet that takes a noisy image and its noise level and outputs class probabilities (85% accurate on nearly clean test images, 64% at σ = 1 \sigma=1 ). For a pair of classes, the order parameter is the classifier’s log-odds z = ℓ a − ℓ b z=\ell_{a}-\ell_{b} , rescaled at each noise level so that the average a a sits at + 1 +1 and the average b b at − 1 -1 . We estimate the distribution of z z across noisy images with a smooth histogram (a kernel density estimate), scan 56 noise levels from high to low until a second hump appears, and fit Equation ( 1 ) there to read off h h . Two details keep the numbers honest. First, statistics that pool many pairs need special care: each class appears in nine of the 45 pairs, so the pairs are not independent. Our confidence intervals therefore resample whole classes ( class-block intervals , 1,000 resamples), and per-pair estimates are medians of 100 bootstrap resamples. Second, an estimated h h is never exactly zero, so we need to know how large it can be by chance. We built pairs of image sets that are exactly symmetric by construction: a class and its vertical flip, or a class and a copy with red and blue channels swapped. We passed them through a classifier trained on them. They give | h | |h| up to 0.047 0.047 , which serves as our noise floor (Appendix D ). The classifier is a measuring stick, and the scale of the stick matters. If we replaced the log-odds z z by a squashed version such as tanh ⁡ ( z / 2 ) \tanh(z/2) , every density transition would move, by a median factor of 4.5 4.5 . What does not depend on the stick is the ordering of class pairs, which is stable across two very different classifier architectures ( r = 0.96 r=0.96 ) and a recalibration ( r = 0.97 r=0.97 ). Nor does any comparison between a model and its data made with the same stick , because two identical distributions look identical under any stick. We rely only on these robust quantities. 3.3. Comparing a model with its data To compare a model with its training data, we record the classifier’s log-odds along the model’s generation trajectories and compare them with the log-odds of real images that have had noise added to them. This is only fair if a perfect model would give exactly the same result as the data. For the stochastic sampler it does: Proposition 1 . Let w c w_{c} be any classifier’s probability for class c c on nearly clean images (noise level σ min \sigma_{\min} ), and let σ > σ min \sigma>\sigma_{\min} . With a perfect score, the distribution of ϕ ⁡ ( x σ ) \phi(x_{\sigma}) along reverse-SDE trajectories, with each trajectory weighted by w a + w b w_{a}+w_{b} at its end point, equals the distribution of ϕ ⁡ ( x σ ) \phi(x_{\sigma}) obtained by adding noise to real images, with each image weighted by w a + w b w_{a}+w_{b} at σ min \sigma_{\min} . The intuition is that the stochastic sampler, run with a perfect score, is the noising process played backwards in time ( Anderson, 1982 ; Haussmann and Pardoux, 1986 ) . Any statement about how an image at one noise level relates to the same image at another noise level is therefore identical on both sides (Appendix A.3 ). The deterministic ODE sampler does not have this property: it produces the right distribution at each noise level, but it links noise levels together differently. We confirmed both facts on a toy problem with three Gaussian classes and an exactly known score. The SDE comparison returns a ratio of 1.00 1.00 ( [ 0.94 , 1.07 ] [0.94,1.07] ), meaning no difference, while the ODE returns 1.36 1.36 ( [ 1.20 , 1.54 ] [1.20,1.54] ). Model and data are always compared at the same sample size, because the smoothing in our histograms depends on it. Two kinds of reweighting appear below. Rebalancing rescales the model’s samples so that the two classes of a pair carry equal weight. Mass-matching goes the other way: it reweights the data so that its class proportions equal the model’s. The second is the cleaner test, because it leaves the model untouched. 3.4. A check of the measuring pipeline If the pipeline works, changing class proportions by a known amount should change h h by half the change in log class ratio, regardless of any model. We checked this on the data alone, reweighting the test images by random known class factors. The slope was 1.00 1.00 ( r = 0.98 r=0.98 , over the 38 pairs whose split was detected both before and after reweighting). Imposing a known imbalance on the model through guidance gave a slope of 1.05 1.05 . These numbers confirm that the classifier behaves like a calibrated likelihood ratio and that the cubic fit is accurate. They say nothing about whether any model is right. 3.5.
